summary: An implementation report for the ForCES protocol, recording how it was implemented and tested for interoperability against the requirements (RFC 3654) and framework (RFC 3746). It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6053 reports on three ForCES implementations and a test of whether they could exchange messages. The tested scenarios succeeded, but the test did not cover the security features.

subtitle: A report on independent ForCES implementations and their interoperability test.

tldr.problem: ForCES needed evidence that independent implementations of its protocol, model, and SCTP transport mapping could work together.
tldr.mechanism: The report surveys three implementations and describes an interoperability test where implementations exchanged messages and protocol analyzers checked them.
tldr.outcome: The tested scenarios succeeded and the implementations interoperated. Security features were not tested. RFC 6053 has been updated by RFC 6984.

today: RFC 6053 is an Informational implementation report and has been updated by RFC 6984. Its results describe the implementations and test reported in the document.

sections.title: Purpose of the Implementation Report
sections.content:
ForCES defines a framework and protocols for exchanging information between the control plane and forwarding plane of a network element. RFC 6053 reports on implementations of the ForCES protocol, model, and SCTP-based Transport Mapping Layer (TML), including an interoperability test.

A Control Element (CE) acts as the master and instructs one or more Forwarding Elements (FEs), which act as slaves. Logical Functional Blocks (LFBs) describe functions in an FE that a CE can configure or query. The SCTP TML carries protocol messages and handles transport matters such as reliability and ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: ForCES separates network-device control from packet forwarding. This report checks whether systems built by different teams could exchange ForCES messages.

sections.title: The Implementation Survey
sections.content:
The report surveyed implementations from NTT Japan, the University of Patras, and Zhejiang Gongshang University. Each respondent marked protocol, model, and SCTP TML features as implemented, planned, or not planned.

The report also counts extensions to Ethereal/Wireshark and tcpdump as implementations because they can inspect and validate ForCES messages. The survey found that all three implementations had the major features, while some other features were still planned. None reported implementing the TML IPsec feature at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors asked three teams which ForCES features their systems supported and which they planned to add. They also used protocol analyzers that could inspect ForCES messages.

sections.title: How the Interoperability Test Worked
sections.content:
The interoperability test took place in July 2009. Three ForCES implementations took part, along with two organizations that extended protocol analyzers. The analyzers were used to check exchanged messages and, in some cases, their meaning.

The test covered setup and teardown, SCTP priority channels, association setup, queries, heartbeat monitoring, configuration, and message batching. The implementation teams also tested a remote connection between China and Greece, including a system behind a NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: The teams ran a set of setup, query, heartbeat, and configuration scenarios between their systems. Packet analyzers helped check what the systems sent.

sections.title: Results and Problems Found
sections.content:
The report says all implementations were interoperable and all planned scenarios succeeded. An additional test of batching also succeeded. The test uncovered issues such as deadlock during teardown, incorrect TLV padding lengths, and failure to ignore an unknown LFB selector; code bugs were fixed during the test.

The remote connection also exposed message loss and retransmission behavior. One ambiguity about which SCTP priority channel to use was resolved in RFC 5811 before its publication. These results apply to the scenarios and features tested in this report.
sections.plainLanguage: The systems passed the tested scenarios. The test also found several code mistakes and one specification ambiguity, giving the teams a chance to fix or clarify them.

sections.title: Security Was Not Tested
sections.content:
The report states that no security features of the ForCES protocol or SCTP TML were tested. Its survey showed that the implementations had not implemented security features, although participants intended to do so.

The report directs readers to RFC 5810 and RFC 5811 for the security considerations of the protocol and transport mapping. The successful interoperability results therefore do not establish that security features interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: The test checked message exchange, not security. Its results do not show whether the security features work between implementations.
